items.q: What single feature most distinguishes the ESP32 from a classic STM32 for connected IoT?
options: Built-in Wi-Fi and Bluetooth/BLE on the chip — no external radio module needed
It is the only MCU with an ADC
items.explain: The ESP32 integrates Wi-Fi + Bluetooth/BLE on-chip (a SoC), making it a single-chip path to the cloud. An STM32 needs an external radio wired over UART.

items.q: For a hard real-time, safety-critical industrial controller, which is often the better choice and why?
options: STM32 — for deterministic timing and rich industrial peripherals (CAN, advanced timers)
items.explain: The ESP32 excels at low-cost wireless connectivity, but for deterministic, safety-critical control the STM32's predictable timing and industrial peripherals (CAN, advanced timers, FPU/DSP) usually win.

items.q: Which toolchains/languages can program an ESP32?
options: Arduino IDE, ESP-IDF (native SDK), and MicroPython
items.explain: The ESP32 has a broad ecosystem: Arduino (C/C++), Espressif's native ESP-IDF, and MicroPython — a key reason for its popularity.

items.q: What is the fundamental difference between ARM Cortex-A and Cortex-M processors?
options: Cortex-A (with an MMU) runs full OSes like Linux (gateways/phones); Cortex-M is a bare-metal/RTOS microcontroller (sensors/real-time)
Cortex-M runs Android; Cortex-A is for microcontrollers
items.explain: Cortex-A ('Application') has an MMU and runs full operating systems — gateways, phones, Raspberry Pi. Cortex-M ('Microcontroller') is low-power, deterministic, bare-metal/RTOS — sensors and end nodes.

items.q: The presence of which hardware unit most directly enables a processor to run a full multi-process OS?
items.explain: An MMU provides virtual memory and process isolation, which a full OS (Linux) requires. Cortex-A has one; Cortex-M does not (only an optional MPU), so it runs bare-metal/RTOS.

items.q: A Raspberry Pi acting as an IoT gateway and an STM32 sensor node typically use which cores, respectively?
items.explain: The Pi gateway runs Linux on a Cortex-A; the STM32 sensor node runs bare-metal/RTOS on a Cortex-M. This maps to the gateway/fog vs perception/edge layers.

items.q: Why is Embedded C usually preferred for production/real-time firmware over MicroPython?
options: It compiles to native machine code — faster, smaller footprint, and more deterministic
items.explain: Embedded C compiles to efficient native code with a tiny footprint and predictable timing — ideal for constrained, real-time production firmware. MicroPython is interpreted on-device (slower, heavier).

items.q: The biggest advantage of MicroPython for IoT development is:
options: Fast, readable, interactive development (REPL) — great for prototyping and teaching
items.explain: MicroPython trades some speed/memory for fast, readable, interactive development (a live REPL on the device) — excellent for prototyping and learning, then often rewritten in C for production.

items.q: Which serial bus is asynchronous (no shared clock) and point-to-point, commonly used for debug consoles and modems?
items.explain: UART is asynchronous (both ends agree on a baud rate, no clock line) and point-to-point (TX↔RX). Used for serial debug and talking to GPS/BLE/Wi-Fi/cellular modems.

items.q: You need to connect many sensors using as few wires as possible, each individually addressable. Which bus fits best?
options: I²C (2 wires shared, devices have addresses)
items.explain: I²C uses just two shared wires (SDA + SCL) for a whole bus of addressed devices — ideal for many sensors on minimal wiring. SPI is faster but needs a select line per device.

items.q: Which bus offers the HIGHEST data rate (full-duplex), at the cost of more wires (MOSI, MISO, SCLK, SS)?
items.explain: SPI is the fastest of the three (full-duplex, tens of MHz) using 4 wires plus a per-device chip-select — used for displays, SD cards, and high-rate sensors.

items.q: Why are interrupts preferred over polling for battery-powered IoT devices?
options: Interrupts let the CPU sleep and wake only when an event occurs — saving power and reacting fast
Interrupts use more energy than polling
items.explain: Polling wastes cycles constantly checking (can't sleep). Interrupts let the MCU sleep until hardware signals an event (then runs a short ISR) — saving power and giving fast, event-driven response.

items.q: A best practice for Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs) is:
options: Make them as long as possible
Keep them short — do the minimum (set a flag/read a register) and handle heavy work in the main loop
Always do network requests inside them
items.explain: ISRs should be short and fast; long ISRs block other interrupts. Do minimal work (set a flag) and defer heavy processing to the main loop. Protect shared data (e.g., mark volatile).

items.q: Which correctly pairs each bus with its wire count?
options: UART = 4 wires, I²C = 2 wires, SPI = 2 wires
UART = 2 wires (TX/RX), I²C = 2 wires (SDA/SCL), SPI = 4 wires (MOSI/MISO/SCLK/SS)
items.explain: UART: 2 wires (TX, RX). I²C: 2 wires (SDA, SCL) shared across addressed devices. SPI: 4 wires (MOSI, MISO, SCLK, SS) plus a select line per extra device.
